5920:
A faction is a group of people inside a larger group who share their own distinct beliefs, goals, or agenda — and who act together as a united bloc, often clashing with other groups within that same larger body.

The single most important thing to understand is that a faction always exists inside something bigger. It is never a standalone group. It is a splinter, a camp, a sub-group — living within a party, an organization, a movement, a government, or any large collection of people.
Breaking It Down with an Example

Imagine a political party of 500 members. Most of them agree on the broad goal — say, winning elections — but they deeply disagree on how. One group of 120 members believes the party should take bold, radical positions. Another group of 150 members believes the party should stay moderate and cautious. Each of these internal camps is a faction. They are not separate parties — they are still inside the same party — but they have their own identity, their own loyalties, and their own push for influence.

This is the classic picture of a faction.

For a group to be called a faction, it generally has these features:

It is a minority within a larger body. A faction is rarely the whole group — it is a portion of it. If a group breaks away completely and becomes independent, it usually stops being called a faction.

It has a shared, distinct interest or viewpoint. The members of a faction are united by something — a belief, a goal, a leader, a policy — that sets them apart from others in the larger group.

It acts together. Factions coordinate. Members support each other, vote together, campaign together, or pressure leadership together. It is an organized bloc, not just a loose set of like-minded individuals.

It often creates tension or conflict. This is perhaps why the word carries a slightly negative flavor. Factions compete for power, influence, or dominance within the larger group. Calling something a faction subtly implies rivalry and internal division.

The word "faction" is not purely neutral — it leans slightly negative. When someone says a group is "split into factions" or that "factional fighting" is tearing an organization apart, there is a sense of disorder, disloyalty, or self-interest at play. Historically, factions have been seen as a threat to unity.

However, the word is also used in a straightforwardly descriptive way — particularly in journalism and political analysis — without strong judgment. You will often read neutral sentences like "the conservative faction of the party" or "rival factions within the military" where the writer is simply describing the reality of a divided group.

The key takeaway: the word does not celebrate the group it describes. It describes division.

In politics, factions are everywhere. Large political parties are almost always divided into factions — for example, a left wing and a right wing within the same party, each pushing the party in a different direction.

In governments and parliaments, competing factions fight over legislation, leadership, and policy. After a revolution or a coup, rival factions often compete violently for control.

In the military, when a country becomes unstable, different armed factions may emerge — each with its own commander, territory, and agenda.

In religions, a religious community may develop factions that disagree over doctrine, practice, or leadership. These sometimes eventually split into separate sects, but while they are still within the same faith community, they are factions.

In corporations and organizations, board members, executives, or employees can form factions that back different strategies or leaders.

In history, you will frequently encounter factions. The Roman Senate was riddled with factions. Revolutionary France was torn apart by factions. Any large, powerful, and consequential human institution tends to develop them.

Faction vs. group: Every faction is a group, but not every group is a faction. "Group" is general and neutral. "Faction" specifically means a competing sub-group inside a larger body.

Faction vs. party: A political party is a standalone organization. A faction exists within a party (or another body). You can have a faction inside a party, but the party itself is not a faction.

Faction vs. sect: A sect is usually religious and often implies a group that has broken away — or is on the verge of breaking away — to form its own independent movement. A faction is still embedded inside the larger group.

Faction vs. clique: A clique is a small, exclusive social group — often used in informal or personal social settings (like a high school clique). A faction is more organized, more purposeful, and used in political or institutional contexts.

Faction vs. bloc: A bloc is similar to a faction but tends to sound more neutral and coordinated — like countries forming a voting bloc at the United Nations. "Faction" carries more of a sense of internal conflict.

Factional (adjective): relating to factions or caused by factions. "The factional disputes weakened the party."

Factionalism (noun): the tendency to divide into factions; a situation where factions dominate and undermine the unity of a group. "Rampant factionalism made it impossible to govern."

Factious (adjective): tending to cause or be part of factional conflict; divisive. This is a more formal and literary word. "A factious senator who constantly stirred up internal conflict."

A faction is an organized group of people within a larger group who share distinct goals or beliefs and act together — often in opposition to others in that same larger body, creating internal division and competition for power or influence.
5921:
To understand factionalism, you first need to understand faction, because factionalism is built on top of it.

Imagine a large group — say, a political party with thousands of members. Over time, not everyone in that party agrees on everything. Some members want radical change; others prefer a slow, careful approach. Some prioritize economic policy; others care most about social issues. Gradually, people with similar views start clustering together, forming a distinct sub-group within the larger group. That sub-group is called a faction.

A faction is not a separate, independent group. It lives inside a larger group. It has its own identity, its own leaders, its own priorities — but it still operates under the roof of the parent group.

Factionalism is the condition, pattern, or culture in which a group is heavily divided into competing factions that rival, undermine, or work against each other — often at the expense of the group's overall unity and shared goals.

Notice the key word: competing. This is what separates factionalism from ordinary disagreement. When factions don't just disagree but actively compete — fighting for power, influence, resources, or dominance — that struggle is factionalism.

Think of it this way. A healthy group can have internal debate and still move forward together. But under factionalism, the internal divisions become so intense and so structured that people are more loyal to their faction than to the group as a whole. The factions start pulling in different directions, and the group's ability to function suffers as a result.

Picture a large nonprofit organization whose mission is to fight climate change. Inside the organization, three groups form over time:

  • One group believes the only real solution is political lobbying and legal pressure on governments.
  • Another group believes grassroots community campaigns are the answer.
  • A third group thinks funding scientific research is the priority.

At first, they debate. But over time, each group starts protecting its own budget, undermining the other groups' proposals, competing to place its own leaders in top positions, and blocking decisions that don't favor their approach. Meetings become battlegrounds. Progress stalls. The original mission gets buried under internal conflict.

That organization is now experiencing factionalism. The factions have stopped cooperating toward a common goal and started fighting each other for dominance. The whole is now weaker than the sum of its parts.

Factionalism is most visible in:

Politics: Political parties are perhaps the most famous breeding ground for factionalism. A ruling party, for instance, might have a conservative wing and a progressive wing that are in constant rivalry — blocking each other's candidates, leaking damaging information, and voting against each other's bills.

Religion: Religious institutions can fracture into factions over matters of doctrine, practice, leadership, or interpretation of scripture. History is full of religious organizations torn apart by factionalism long before any formal split or schism ever happened.

Workplaces and Organizations: Corporations, universities, NGOs, and government agencies all experience factionalism. Departments compete for resources. Leadership teams split into rival camps. Loyalty to a particular manager or ideology overtakes loyalty to the institution.

Movements: Social and political movements — revolutionary groups, independence movements, activist organizations — are extremely vulnerable to factionalism because they often bring together passionate people with overlapping but not identical visions. History has shown that movements can be destroyed from within by factionalism even when they face little external threat.
The tone of the word — is it negative?

Almost always, yes. Factionalism carries a strongly negative connotation. When someone accuses a group of factionalism, they are criticizing it. They are saying the group has lost discipline, unity, and common purpose — that personal or sub-group interests have overridden the collective good.

However, the intensity of the negativity can vary. In a mild sense, factionalism might simply mean there is troublesome internal rivalry. In a severe sense — especially in political or historical contexts — it can suggest that a group has become so divided that it is essentially self-destructing.
The crucial distinction: disagreement vs. factionalism

This is an important line to draw, because not all internal conflict is factionalism.

Healthy disagreement means members of a group debate, argue, and challenge each other — but they remain united under a shared identity and ultimately work toward the same goals. This is normal and even productive.

Factionalism is when the disagreement hardens into organized, entrenched rivalry. It's when the competing sides stop being "people with different opinions" and start being "rival camps with their own loyalties, leaders, and agendas." It's when the internal division becomes the defining feature of the group, and when people prioritize their faction's success over the group's success.

The line, in short, is between debating together and fighting against each other from within.

Factionalism exists on a spectrum.

At its mild end, it might just mean a group is somewhat disorganized and inefficient because of internal competition.

At its severe end, factionalism can destroy organizations, collapse governments, end political movements, trigger civil wars, and cause religious institutions to violently tear themselves apart. Many of history's most consequential collapses — of empires, parties, and revolutions — were accelerated or directly caused by factionalism from within.

• Faction (noun) — the sub-group itself. "There are three factions within the party."
  • Factional (adjective) — relating to or caused by factions. "Factional conflict is tearing the movement apart."
  • Factionalist (noun) — a person who promotes or engages in factionalism. "The party expelled known factionalists."
  • Factionalize (verb) — to divide into factions. "The dispute began to factionalize the organization."

Factionalism is the destructive pattern in which a group splinters into competing internal sub-groups (factions) that prioritize their own power and interests over the unity and common goals of the group as a whole.
5922:
Factious describes a person, group, or atmosphere that causes or promotes internal division and conflict within a larger group — usually by pushing a narrow self-serving agenda over the common good, and by forming or encouraging competing factions that fight against each other from the inside.

Think of a team, a political party, a country, or any organization. Now imagine some people within that group who constantly stir up disagreement, form rival camps, pull in opposite directions, and undermine the group's unity — not because the cause is righteous, but out of self-interest, ambition, or spite. That behavior — and those people — are factious.

The word almost always carries a negative tone. To call someone factious is to accuse them of being a destructive force from within.

The word comes from the idea of a faction — a small, self-interested group within a larger group that pursues its own goals at the expense of everyone else. When you call someone or something factious, you're saying they belong to that world, or that they actively create it.

So:

  • A factious politician is one who splits their own party with constant in-fighting rather than uniting it.
  • A factious group is one that tears an organization apart from the inside through rivalry and discord.
  • A factious spirit describes a general mood of internal rebellion and disunity in a place or institution.

This is where many people get confused, so let's be precise:

Factious ≠ Fractious.
These two look and sound similar but mean different things. Fractious means irritable, cranky, or unruly — like a tired toddler or a restless crowd. Factious specifically means causing internal division and group conflict. A fractious person is just difficult to deal with. A factious person actively fractures the unity of a group.

Factious ≠ Contentious.
Something contentious causes controversy or strong disagreement — it could be a topic, a policy, or an opinion. Factious is not about a topic being divisive; it's about a person or group that creates division as a pattern of behavior.

Factious ≠ Seditious.
Seditious means inciting rebellion against a ruling authority or government. Factious is broader — it applies to any group (a company, a church, a sports club, a senate) where internal quarreling breaks out. You don't need a government for something to be factious.

Imagine a neighborhood committee formed to improve the local park. Most members want to cooperate and get things done. But two or three members keep forming opposing camps, rallying others to their side, blocking each other's proposals, spreading gossip, and making everything about winning rather than about the park. Those members are being factious. The committee has become factious. The whole thing might collapse because of this factious spirit.

This is exactly the kind of behavior the word describes — internal rivalry that poisons a collective effort.

Here are sentences that show the word in action across different settings:

  • "The factious senators spent more time fighting each other than governing the country."
  • "Her factious tendencies made every team she joined collapse into rival cliques."
  • "The club's factious atmosphere drove away members who simply wanted to enjoy the hobby in peace."
  • "History shows that factious nobles weakened many kingdoms from within long before any foreign enemy arrived."
  • "He was a talented leader, but his factious spirit made cooperation impossible."
Strength and Tone of the Word

Factious is a strong, formal word with a clearly negative charge. You would typically find it in serious writing — history books, political commentary, formal essays, or literary fiction. It's not a word you'd toss casually into everyday conversation, but when it appears, it carries real weight. It signals not just that people disagree, but that they are actively tearing a group apart from the inside through organized, persistent, self-serving conflict.
If you ever need to recall this word quickly: factious = causing destructive internal division within a group, usually through selfish rivalry and the formation of competing camps.
5923:
Factitious means artificially created, deliberately manufactured, or contrived — rather than arising naturally, spontaneously, or genuinely.

When something is factitious, it didn't come about on its own. Someone made it happen, forced it into existence, or put it on — and because of that, it lacks authenticity. Think of it as the opposite of something that is natural, organic, or genuine.

Imagine a garden where wildflowers grow on their own in spring — that's natural. Now imagine someone buying plastic flowers and sticking them into the ground to look like a garden — that's factitious. The appearance is there, but the reality underneath it isn't.

The word captures two things at once:

  • Something was deliberately produced (by human action or effort), and
  • Because of that, it feels unreal, forced, or inauthentic

1. Emotions and Behaviour

This is the most common everyday use. When someone's reaction or feeling isn't genuine but is put on for effect, it's factitious.

  • "The celebrity's tears at the press conference seemed factitious — a calculated move to win public sympathy."
  • "He greeted everyone with factitious warmth, smiling broadly at people he clearly had no interest in."
  • "The excitement in the room felt factitious, as if everyone had been coached on how to react."

The people in these examples aren't necessarily lying outright. They're performing an emotion rather than feeling it.

2. Demand, Value, or Prosperity (Economics/Social Commentary)

When something like economic growth, popularity, or market demand is artificially stimulated — rather than driven by real, underlying forces — it can be called factitious.

  • "The housing boom was factitious, propped up by cheap credit rather than genuine demand."
  • "Her fame was factitious, a product of relentless marketing rather than real talent."

3. Medicine — Factitious Disorder

This is a specific, important clinical use. A factitious disorder is a psychological condition in which a person deliberately fabricates, exaggerates, or even causes illness in themselves — not to gain any obvious external benefit (like avoiding work or getting money), but because of psychological need. They are genuinely playing the role of a sick person, manufacturing symptoms intentionally.

There is also factitious disorder imposed on another (previously called Munchausen syndrome by proxy), where someone — usually a caregiver — deliberately causes or fakes illness in another person (often a child) under their care.

The word "factitious" fits perfectly here: the illness is manufactured, not natural.
The Distinction You Must Know: Factitious vs. Fictitious

This is the single biggest source of confusion with this word, and getting it right will set you apart.

Fictitiousmeans imaginary or invented — something that doesn't exist at all, like a fictional character or a made-up story.
Factitiousmeans artificially produced — something that does exist in some form, but was deliberately manufactured rather than arising naturally.

Here's the clearest way to feel the difference:

  • A dragon is fictitious — it's completely made up; it doesn't exist.
  • A smile you force when you don't feel happy is factitious — the smile is real, it actually exists on your face, but it was artificially produced, not a genuine expression of joy.

Another example:

  • A ghost in a novel is fictitious — purely imaginary.
  • Artificially inflated crowd noise pumped into a sports broadcast is factitious — the sound really exists, it's just not natural; it was manufactured.

So: fictitious = not real. Factitious = real, but manufactured / not natural.
The Full Feeling of the Word

When you call something factitious, you're subtly implying a criticism — that there is a gap between what something appears to be and what it truly is. It carries a slight negative or suspicious tone. It suggests someone or something is being inauthentic, even if not outright lying.

It pairs naturally with words like: enthusiasm, affection, demand, kindness, unity, cheerfulness, crisis, illness — basically, any state that is supposed to arise naturally but has instead been manufactured for effect.

• "The politician's concern for ordinary people appeared factitious, given his record in office."
  • "Her factitious laughter made everyone uncomfortable — it was clearly forced."
  • "The national unity after the scandal was factitious, papering over deep divisions."
  • "Doctors suspected a factitious disorder when no medical explanation could be found for his repeated hospitalizations."
  • "The product's glowing reputation was factitious, built on paid reviews."
One-Line Summary to Lock It In

Factitious = artificially made or forced into being, and therefore lacking genuine authenticity.

If something grew on its own, it's natural. If something was deliberately manufactured to seem real or genuine — that's factitious.
5924: "Factoid" has two meanings in modern English — and they are nearly opposite to each other. This split is real, documented, and the source of genuine confusion. Understanding both is the whole game.
The original, strict meaning — a false claim dressed up as fact

In its original sense, a factoid is a piece of false or unverified information that looks like a fact, gets repeated widely and confidently, and therefore starts to feel true — even though it isn't.

The "-oid" in "factoid" signals "resembling" or "fake version of." Just like a humanoid looks like a human but isn't one, a factoid looks like a fact but isn't one. It has the costume of truth without the substance.

The critical quality is the masquerade: a factoid isn't just wrong — it's wrong in a way that convinces people it's right. It circulates as though it were established fact.

Example:
"The claim that we only use 10% of our brain is a classic factoid — it sounds credible, gets repeated endlessly, but is completely false."

Here, calling it a factoid is almost an accusation: this thing pretends to be a fact, but it isn't.
The second, popular meaning — a small, trivial true fact

Over decades, especially through media and casual speech, "factoid" drifted into a second usage: a brief, interesting, or trivial piece of information that happens to be true — essentially a "fun fact." Something minor, surprising, or entertaining.

Example:
"Here's a fun factoid: a group of flamingos is called a 'flamboyance.'"

Here, the speaker isn't doubting the information at all — they're presenting it as a genuine (if small and quirky) truth.
Why this matters — the genuine conflict

These two meanings pull in opposite directions:

  • Original meaning: something false that is mistaken for fact
  • Popular meaning: something true but minor and trivial

If someone says "that's just a factoid," they might mean "that's not actually true" — or they might mean "that's a small, trivial piece of trivia." The same word, two contradictory readings.

Both meanings are now listed in major dictionaries like Merriam-Webster and Oxford, which is why neither can be called outright "wrong." But this is precisely what makes the word slippery.

Because of this split, careful writers and editors still tend to use "factoid" in its original sense — a false belief that circulates as fact. Using it to mean "fun fact" risks confusing careful readers, who may silently note the loose usage.

If you mean a small, interesting true fact, it's cleaner and clearer to just say "fun fact," "trivia," or "interesting detail." That leaves no room for misreading.

If you mean a false claim that people widely believe, "factoid" is the perfect, precise word for it.

A factoid, strictly speaking, is a false claim that wears the disguise of a fact — repeated and believed, but untrue. Loosely (and very commonly), it means a small, interesting, true piece of information. The word lives at a genuine fork in the language. Knowing both meanings — and the tension between them — is what it means to truly understand this word.
5925:
A factor is anything that plays a part in producing a result or making something happen the way it does.

Think of baking a cake. The result — how the cake turns out — depends on several things: the flour, the oven temperature, how long you bake it, the quality of your eggs. Each of these is a factor. None of them alone bakes the cake, but each one influences the final outcome. Change any one of them, and the cake changes too.

That's exactly what a factor is in everyday life: one of the elements, conditions, or causes that together bring about a result.

Some examples:

  • "Lack of sleep is a major factor in poor concentration."
  • "Several factors led to the company's failure."
  • "Diet and exercise are key factors in good health."

Notice that we almost always say "a factor" or "one factor" — not "the factor." This is because factors rarely work alone. They exist alongside other factors. When you want to point to the single most important one, you'd call it the deciding factor or the key factor.

The word "factor" carries one essential idea — something that contributes to an outcome — but it shows up in different contexts with slightly different flavors.

1. A Cause or Contributor (most common use)

This is the everyday meaning. A factor is a circumstance, condition, or element that influences or helps produce something.

  • "Her experience was a major factor in getting her hired."
  • "Poverty is a significant factor in many social problems."
  • "Time is a factor we haven't considered."

A key nuance: saying something is "a factor" doesn't mean it's the only cause — it means it's one of the causes or influences. This makes the word precise and honest, because most results in life have multiple causes.

Types you'll often hear:

  • Contributing factor — something that helps bring about a result but didn't cause it all on its own. ("Stress was a contributing factor in his illness.")
  • Deciding/determining factor — the one element that ultimately tips the balance and settles the outcome. ("The deciding factor was price.")
  • Key/major factor — a particularly important one among several. ("Trust is a key factor in any relationship.")
  • Limiting factor — something that acts as a ceiling or barrier, stopping further progress. ("In this region, water is the limiting factor for crop growth." Once water runs out, it doesn't matter how much sunlight there is — growth stops.)
  • Risk factor — something that increases the likelihood of a bad outcome, especially in medicine. ("Smoking is a risk factor for cancer." It doesn't guarantee cancer, but it makes it more probable.)
  • X factor — an unknown, mysterious, or hard-to-define quality that seems to make someone or something special or successful. ("She has the X factor — audiences love her and no one can quite explain why.")

2. In Mathematics

In math, "factor" has a sharper, more technical meaning: a number (or expression) that divides evenly into another number, with nothing left over.

If you multiply two numbers together to get a third number, both of those two numbers are factors of the third.

  • 3 × 4 = 12 → so 3 and 4 are factors of 12
  • 2 × 6 = 12 → so 2 and 6 are also factors of 12
  • The complete list of factors of 12 is: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12

Every number on that list divides into 12 without leaving a remainder.

An important special case: prime factors. A prime number is a number divisible only by 1 and itself (like 2, 3, 5, 7, 11...). The prime factors of a number are the prime numbers that multiply together to give you that number.

  • Prime factors of 12: 2 × 2 × 3 (because 2 × 2 × 3 = 12, and 2 and 3 are both prime)

This mathematical sense of "factor" is closely related to the general sense: just as contributing factors "make up" a result in real life, mathematical factors "make up" a number through multiplication.

3. In Science and Medicine

Scientists often use "factor" to refer to a specific measurable element or substance that plays a role in a biological or physical process.

  • Clotting factors are proteins in the blood that work together to stop bleeding when you're injured. People with hemophilia are missing certain clotting factors.
  • Growth factors are substances in the body that signal cells to grow, divide, or develop.
  • Risk factors (mentioned above) are widely used in medicine to identify what increases someone's probability of developing a disease.

In scientific writing, this word signals that something is one identifiable piece of a larger, more complex process.

4. In Business and Finance

Historically, a factor was a person who acted as an agent for someone else — buying and selling goods on their behalf. This is an older use, but it survives in one important modern form:

In finance, a factor (also called a factoring company) is a financial institution that buys a company's unpaid invoices. If a business is owed money by its customers but needs cash right now, it can sell those invoices to a factor at a small discount. The factor then collects the full payment from the customers later. This whole process is called factoring.

You're unlikely to encounter "factor" in this business sense unless you're reading about trade, finance, or economic history.

It helps to understand how "factor" compares to words that mean similar things:

  • Cause: A cause directly produces an effect. A factor contributes to an effect. All causes are factors, but not all factors are causes. ("The virus was the cause of his illness; stress and poor diet were factors.")
  • Element: An element is a component or part of something. It's vaguer than "factor" and doesn't imply influence on an outcome. You'd say "water is an element of the solution" but "dehydration was a factor in his fatigue."
  • Variable: Used mostly in science and statistics. A variable is something that can change and is being measured or studied. Factors influence outcomes; variables are what you observe and measure. In practice, these words often overlap.
  • Component: A component is a physical or structural part of a whole. ("The engine is a component of the car.") A factor is about influence, not physical parts.

A factor is one of the things that contributes to a result. Whether you're talking about why someone succeeded, why a business failed, how a number breaks down in mathematics, or what increases the risk of a disease — if something plays a role in producing the outcome, it's a factor.

The word is precise because it automatically implies that there are usually multiple factors at work, and it leaves room for that complexity rather than forcing a single, oversimplified explanation onto things.
5926:
To factor in something means to include it as one of the important things you think about when making a decision, plan, or calculation.

Think of it this way: when you are deciding something or working something out, there are several things you need to consider. Each one of those things is a factor — a piece of the puzzle. When you factor something in, you are making sure that piece of the puzzle is not forgotten or ignored — you are putting it into your thinking.
Breaking Down the Word "Factor"

Before you can truly master "factor in," you need to understand the word "factor" itself.

A factor is simply a thing that plays a role in producing a result. It is one element among several that together influence an outcome.

For example:

  • Weather is a factor in deciding whether to go on a picnic.
  • Price is a factor in deciding which phone to buy.
  • Distance is a factor in deciding which school to attend.

None of these things alone makes the decision for you, but each one contributes to it. That is what a factor is — a contributing element.

Now, when you factor something in, you are saying: "I am making sure this element is part of my thinking. I am not ignoring it."
The Phrase as a Whole

"Factor in" is a phrasal verb — that is, a verb made up of two words (a verb + a small word like "in," "out," "up," etc.) that together create a specific meaning.

To factor in = to include and account for something when making a calculation, decision, or plan.

The opposite phrase is "factor out," which means to deliberately exclude something from your thinking or calculation.
Simple, Everyday Examples

Let's look at "factor in" in real-life situations:

1. Planning a trip:

"We need to factor in the cost of the hotel when planning our budget."

→ The hotel cost is one of the things they must include and think about. They shouldn't forget it.

2. Cooking a meal for guests:

"She factored in that two of her guests were vegetarian when planning the menu."

→ She included that important detail in her planning so that everyone could eat.

3. Commuting to work:

"He factored in the traffic when deciding what time to leave."

→ He didn't just think about how long the drive normally takes. He also included the likely traffic delay in his calculation.

4. Buying a car:

"Don't forget to factor in the insurance and maintenance costs, not just the price of the car itself."

→ The total cost of owning the car is more than just the purchase price. The insurance and maintenance costs must also be included in the calculation.

5. Business decision:

"The company factored in the possibility of rising inflation before setting their prices for next year."

→ They considered inflation as a real possibility and let it shape their decision.
The Key Idea Behind Every Example

In every single case above, there is a central activity happening — making a plan, a decision, or a calculation. And in each case, "factoring in" means:

"This is a relevant piece of information, and I am making sure it is part of my thinking — not left out."

The danger that "factor in" protects against is oversight — forgetting something important that could affect your outcome.
Grammar: How to Use It Correctly

"Factor in" is a transitive phrasal verb, which means it always needs an object — the thing being factored in. You cannot just say "we should factor in" and leave it hanging. You must say what is being factored in.

Pattern 1: Factor in + [the thing]

"You should factor in the extra time needed for editing."

Pattern 2: Factor + [the thing] + in

The two words of a phrasal verb can often be split, with the object placed in the middle. This is perfectly natural and common:

"You should factor the extra time in."

Both patterns are correct. However, when the object is a pronoun (it, them, this, etc.), you must split the verb — the pronoun always goes in the middle:

✅ "Don't forget to factor it in."
❌ "Don't forget to factor in it." ← This sounds wrong.
Tenses — All Forms of the Verb

TenseExample

Here are the forms in plain text:

  • Present: "We always factor in the weather when planning outdoor events."
  • Past: "They factored in the delay when calculating the delivery time."
  • Future: "We will factor in your feedback before publishing the final version."
  • Present perfect: "She has already factored in all the risks."
  • Continuous (ongoing): "The team is factoring in all the new data as it comes in."
Synonyms — Other Ways to Say the Same Thing

These phrases carry the same or very similar meaning:

  • Take into account → "Take the extra cost into account."
  • Take into consideration → "Take the weather into consideration."
  • Account for → "Make sure you account for the time difference."
  • Allow for → "Allow for some delays."
  • Bear in mind → "Bear in mind that prices may change."
  • Include → "Include all hidden costs."

All of these phrases share the same spirit: don't ignore this — make it part of your thinking.

Among all of these, "factor in" tends to feel slightly more precise and analytical — as if you are treating something like a variable in a formula. It is popular in business, finance, and formal writing, but it is equally common in casual speech.
The Opposite: "Factor Out"

Just as you can factor in (include something), you can also factor out (exclude or remove something from consideration):

"When comparing the two candidates, the interviewer tried to factor out any personal bias."

→ She tried to remove personal bias from her evaluation so it wouldn't influence her judgement.

"Factor out the shipping cost, and the product itself is actually quite affordable."

→ If you don't count the shipping, the product is cheap.
Register: Formal, Informal, or Both?

"Factor in" works comfortably in both formal and informal settings. You will hear it in:

  • A boardroom: "We need to factor in the regulatory changes before finalising the budget."
  • A casual conversation: "Did you factor in parking when you planned how long it would take?"
  • Academic writing: "Studies must factor in the participants' age and health history."
  • Everyday planning: "Factor in some rest time — you've been working non-stop."

It is a versatile phrase that never sounds out of place.
A Very Common Mistake to Avoid

A common mistake is forgetting the object. Remember, you must always say what you are factoring in:

❌ "We should probably factor in before making the decision."
✅ "We should probably factor in the risks before making the decision."

Another mistake is confusing "factor in" with simply "consider." While they are close in meaning, "factor in" has a stronger sense of mathematically or systematically including something in a whole picture, whereas "consider" is broader and less precise. Both are correct in many situations, but "factor in" carries the feeling of calculation and completeness.
Summary in One Sentence

To "factor in" something means to include it as an important element in your thinking, planning, or calculation — making sure it is not overlooked when you are working toward a conclusion or decision.
5927:
A factotum is a person who does all sorts of different tasks for someone else — a general all-purpose helper who handles whatever needs to be done, rather than having one specific job.

Think of it this way. If you hire a plumber, they fix pipes. If you hire a chef, they cook. But a factotum? They do a bit of everything. They might fix the pipes and cook and run errands and manage your schedule. Their defining quality is not skill in one area, but availability and flexibility across many areas.

The relationship it implies: A factotum almost always works for someone. There is usually a more important or powerful person at the center — a boss, an employer, an aristocrat, a celebrity — and the factotum orbits around that person, handling all the tasks that person doesn't want to deal with themselves. In this sense, a factotum is deeply tied to service.

The tone of the word: "Factotum" sits in an interesting middle ground. It is not insulting, but it is not entirely flattering either. Calling someone a factotum can suggest they are indispensable and capable — a real jack-of-all-trades. But it can also subtly suggest that the person is a bit of an errand-runner, someone who does whatever they are told without a clearly defined role or status of their own. The tone depends heavily on context, and the word itself is fairly neutral on the surface.

It is also worth knowing that "factotum" feels like a formal, slightly old-fashioned word. You are more likely to encounter it in literary writing, historical fiction, or journalism than in everyday conversation. When someone uses it, they are being precise and somewhat sophisticated in their word choice.

"The aging novelist relied entirely on his factotum, who answered his letters, drove him to appointments, and even chose his meals."

Here, the factotum is clearly a devoted all-purpose assistant who handles the novelist's entire practical life.

"She had spent twenty years as a factotum for the law firm, doing everything from legal research to ordering office supplies."

Here, the word suggests someone whose role was never clearly defined — they simply did whatever was needed.

"The king's factotum was more powerful than any minister, because he alone knew every secret and managed every detail of the royal household."

Here, the word is used almost admiringly — the factotum's power comes precisely from being trusted with everything.

How it differs from similar words: A secretary handles communications and scheduling. An assistant helps with specific tasks. A butler manages a household. A servant performs domestic duties. A factotum can overlap with all of these, but the key difference is range. A factotum is defined by the fact that they do everything, not that they specialize in any one thing. That breadth is the whole point of the word.

Can it refer to things, not just people? Occasionally, writers use "factotum" metaphorically to describe a thing that serves many purposes — a tool, a department, or an institution that handles all kinds of functions. But this is less common. The word is most naturally and most powerfully used for a person.

In short: A factotum is the person behind a more important person, quietly keeping everything running — the one who handles everything so their employer doesn't have to handle anything. Capable, versatile, often indispensable, but rarely in the spotlight.
5928: The word faculty means a power, ability, or capacity — or a group of people with a shared role or subject area. These two broad directions (ability vs. group) cover almost every use of this word you will ever encounter.
Meaning 1: A natural power or ability of the mind or body

This is the oldest and most philosophically rich meaning. A faculty is a natural, built-in power that a person possesses simply by being human — a capacity you are born with or develop as part of your nature.

These can be mental or physical.

Examples of mental faculties:

  • The faculty of reason — the ability to think logically
  • The faculty of memory — the ability to retain and recall information
  • The faculty of judgment — the ability to assess situations and make sound decisions
  • The faculty of imagination — the ability to form mental images and ideas
  • The faculty of perception — the ability to be aware of things through the senses

Examples of physical faculties:

  • The faculty of speech — the ability to speak
  • The faculty of sight — the ability to see
  • The faculty of hearing — the ability to hear

Example sentences:

  • "Language is a faculty unique to humans."
  • "Even at 90, her faculty of reason remained completely sharp."

The plural — "faculties" — is especially important

When people say "one's faculties," they almost always mean a person's full range of mental powers working normally. This phrase is very commonly used to describe whether someone is mentally sharp or not:

  • "He is still in full possession of his faculties." → He is mentally sharp and clear.
  • "She is not in her right faculties." → Something is wrong with her normal mental functioning.
  • "The patient has begun losing his faculties." → His mental abilities are declining, perhaps due to illness or old age.

This is one of the most frequently encountered uses of this word, so recognise it well.
Meaning 2: A particular personal talent or aptitude

Related to Meaning 1, but a little more personal. Here, faculty refers to a specific natural gift or talent that a particular person seems to have — something they do easily and naturally, almost effortlessly.

Examples:

  • "She has a faculty for making people feel instantly welcome."
  • "He has a remarkable faculty for learning languages quickly."
  • "She has a faculty for spotting problems before they grow."

How is this different from Meaning 1?

Meaning 1 talks about powers that all humans share (everyone has the faculty of memory, everyone has the faculty of reason). Meaning 2 talks about a special, personal gift that you specifically seem to have more of than others.
Meaning 3: A department or division of a university (especially British English)

In the academic world — particularly in British English, European universities, and many universities around the world — a faculty is a large division of a university organised around a broad subject area.

Think of it like a major branch of the university tree.

Examples:

  • Faculty of Medicine
  • Faculty of Law
  • Faculty of Arts and Humanities
  • Faculty of Engineering
  • Faculty of Social Sciences

Example sentences:

  • "She is studying in the Faculty of Medicine at Oxford."
  • "He transferred to the Faculty of Law in his second year."
  • "The Faculty of Arts is hosting a public lecture tomorrow."

Within a faculty, there are usually smaller departments (e.g., within the Faculty of Arts, you might have the Department of English, the Department of History, etc.).
Meaning 4: The teaching staff of a school or university (especially American English)

In American English, the word faculty is very commonly used to refer to the entire body of teachers and professors at a school, college, or university — not a department, but the people themselves.

Examples:

  • "The faculty voted to adopt the new grading policy."
  • "She joined the faculty of Yale University as a professor of biology."
  • "A meeting was held for all faculty and staff."
  • "He is a member of the faculty at the local community college."

Notice that in this meaning, "faculty" acts almost like a collective noun, similar to words like "staff" or "team." You can say "the faculty is" or "the faculty are" depending on whether you treat them as one unit or as many individuals.
Meaning 5: A licence or special authority (formal, legal, or church contexts)

This meaning is rare in everyday conversation, but you may encounter it in formal, legal, or ecclesiastical (church-related) writing. Here, a faculty is an official permission or authorisation granted to someone to do something they would not otherwise be legally or officially allowed to do.

Examples:

  • In the Church of England, a faculty is a formal legal permission granted by church authorities to make changes to a church building (e.g., adding a new feature, altering the structure).
  • A professional body may grant a faculty to a practitioner, authorising them to practise in a specific area.

Example sentence:

  • "A faculty was granted by the diocese for the installation of a new organ in the church."

You will mostly see this in legal, historical, or church documents. In day-to-day speech, this meaning is uncommon.
Quick summary of all meanings at a glance

#What "faculty" meansContext
1A natural power/ability of the mind or bodyGeneral use — very common
2A particular personal talent or giftGeneral use — common
3A major division/department of a universityAcademic (especially British/global)
4The teaching staff of a school or universityAcademic (especially American)
5An official licence or special authorityFormal/legal/church — rare
How to tell which meaning is intended

Because context does most of the work, here are simple clues:

  • If the sentence is about what a person can do mentally or physically → Meaning 1 or 2
  • If the sentence is about "one's faculties" → Meaning 1 (mental sharpness)
  • If the sentence is about a university unit → Meaning 3 (department) or Meaning 4 (staff)
  • If British/international academic context → likely Meaning 3
  • If American academic context → likely Meaning 4
  • If in a formal legal or church document → Meaning 5

The word can sometimes be used in a slightly poetic or elevated way in general writing, just to mean "a remarkable ability":

  • "He seemed to possess an almost supernatural faculty for predicting what people would do next."

This sits between Meanings 1 and 2 — it's describing an extraordinary capacity, and you will understand it perfectly well using what you have already learned.
5929:
To understand faddish, you first need to understand a fad.

A fad is something — a trend, a style, a habit, a product, an idea — that suddenly becomes wildly popular, spreads fast like a fire, and then dies out just as quickly, often leaving people wondering why they ever cared about it in the first place. It is a short-lived craze. Think of it as the opposite of something "timeless" or "classic."

Faddish is simply the adjective form of fad. It means: having the qualities of a fad — that is, something that is trendy right now but unlikely to last, or appealing to people's desire to follow the latest craze rather than having genuine, lasting value.

When you call something faddish, you are making two observations at once:

  1. It is currently popular or trendy.
  2. Its popularity is shallow and temporary — it will likely fade soon.

So the word captures both the shine of something new and the doubt that it will stick around.

Faddish almost always carries a mildly critical or skeptical tone. When you call something faddish, you are subtly suggesting:

  • It lacks deep, lasting value.
  • People are following it because it is fashionable, not because it is genuinely good or useful.
  • It is driven more by hype than by substance.

It is not a harsh insult, but it is not a compliment either. It is a quiet way of raising an eyebrow at something.

Faddish can describe both things and people.

1. Describing Things

When a thing (a product, idea, diet, style, activity, etc.) is called faddish, it means that thing is popular right now but is expected to lose its appeal soon.

  • "The juice cleanse trend feels faddish to me — people were obsessed with it for a year, and now nobody talks about it."
  • "That restaurant serves faddish food — the kind that looks great on social media but won't be popular in two years."
  • "Some critics worry that this new teaching method is faddish rather than truly effective."

2. Describing People

When a person is called faddish, it means they are someone who eagerly follows every new trend without much thought — they jump from one craze to the next.

  • "She is quite faddish — last month it was hot yoga, this month it is cold plunging, and who knows what next month will bring."
  • "He has a faddish personality; he never sticks with anything long enough to master it."
The Key Qualities That Make Something Faddish

If you want to recognize whether something is faddish, look for these signs:

  • Sudden rise in popularity — it seemingly came out of nowhere.
  • Everyone is doing or talking about it — there is a herd mentality behind it.
  • No deep roots — it lacks a long track record or strong evidence of lasting benefit.
  • Driven by novelty — people like it because it is new, not because it is genuinely superior.
  • Quick to fade — after the hype dies down, people quietly move on.

Faddish is a moderate word — it is not extreme. Here is a rough scale to help you place it:

Timeless → Classic → Trendy → Faddish → A passing craze → Completely forgotten

So "faddish" sits in the space where something is clearly trendy but already hints at being temporary and somewhat hollow.

• It is not the same as "popular." Something can be popular and still have lasting value (e.g., reading books is popular and timeless — not faddish). Faddish popularity is shallow and short.
  • It is not the same as "new." Many new things are genuinely groundbreaking and here to stay. Faddish things are new and suspected to be temporary.
  • It is not the same as "bad." A faddish thing might actually be enjoyable or even somewhat useful — the point is simply that its popularity won't endure.

These words share meaning with faddish and can help you understand it from different angles:

  • Trendy — currently popular (but less skeptical in tone than faddish)
  • Fleeting — lasting only a short time
  • Passing — not permanent (e.g., "a passing craze")
  • Fashionable — in style right now (more neutral than faddish)
  • Gimmicky — relying on novelty or tricks rather than real value (slightly stronger criticism than faddish)

These words mean the opposite of faddish:

  • Timeless — never goes out of style
  • Enduring — lasts a long time
  • Classic — proven, lasting, respected over time
  • Evergreen — always relevant, never outdated
Faddish describes something (or someone) that is caught up in short-lived trends — currently popular, but lacking the depth or staying power to last, and followed more out of hype than genuine worth.
